title: The Capital Order Problem: Why the Most Expensive Money Gets Raised First
excerpt: Growing businesses often reach for equity before they have exhausted cheaper capital. The order it is raised in matters as much as the amount, and most owners have never mapped it out.
content:
October has most growing businesses thinking past this financial year, toward the next vehicle, the next hire, the next site, or the acquisition that keeps coming up in conversation. The question that gets asked first is usually how much this will cost and where the money will come from. The question that matters just as much, and gets asked far less often, is what order to raise it in.

Most owner-led businesses treat capital as one pool. Money is money, and the job is simply to find enough of it. In practice, every dollar of funding carries a different cost, a different amount of control given up, and a different claim on everything the business earns from here. Raised in the wrong order, growth capital can quietly become the most expensive decision a business makes all year, even when the growth itself turns out to be exactly the right call.

The pattern we typically see across East Coast SMEs runs close to backwards. Equity conversations start early, debt gets treated as a last resort, and the cheapest capital already sitting inside the business goes untouched. Getting this right starts well before any lender or investor conversation, which is exactly what a proper capital raise preparation process is designed to surface.

What Each Dollar of Capital Actually Costs

Retained profit reinvested into the business is the cheapest capital available, because the only cost is what else that cash could have done. Finance tied to a specific asset or to receivables, equipment finance, invoice or debtor finance, comes next, priced against something tangible rather than the whole business, and usually settled as soon as that asset or invoice is paid out. Bank term debt sits above that, still finite and still repaid on a fixed schedule, but priced against the strength of the whole balance sheet rather than a single asset, which is why it takes longer to arrange and carries more conditions. Mezzanine finance costs more again, because a lender is taking a risk closer to an owner's risk without actually becoming one, and the pricing reflects that extra exposure. Equity is the most expensive capital a business can raise, not because the cheque is large, but because it is permanent. It is not a cost for this year. It is a share of every year of profit the business produces from the day the raise completes, whether that year is a good one or a difficult one.

Why the Order Gets Reversed

What we typically see is not an owner choosing expensive capital carelessly. It is the sequence collapsing under time pressure. A bank may have already said no on serviceability grounds before cheaper, asset-specific options were explored properly. A shareholder or investor conversation that is already underway can feel like the path of least resistance compared with the slower work of structuring debt correctly, especially when that investor is someone the owner already knows and trusts. And growth decisions rarely arrive with a calm runway. A contract, a site or an acquisition usually comes with its own deadline attached. By the time the capital is actually needed, there is often no time left to work through the cheaper options first, so the fastest yes becomes the one that gets taken, regardless of what it costs the business over the following five years.

Building the Stack in the Right Order

The businesses that fund growth well tend to work through the same sequence every time, almost as a habit rather than a one-off decision. They start by asking what retained profit or existing facilities can already cover, and whether capital currently tied up elsewhere in the business could be redeployed first. Then they look at whether the growth itself, the equipment, the stock, the receivables, can be financed directly against the asset it creates, rather than against the business as a whole. Only once those options are exhausted does bank term debt get sized against serviceability, with mezzanine considered for whatever gap remains between what the bank will lend and what the business actually needs. Equity is the last call, not the first, and only for the portion that genuinely cannot be funded any other way. A Capital Raise Feasibility assessment exists for exactly this moment, working out which instrument actually fits before any conversation with a lender or investor begins.

Getting the order right rarely changes how much a business raises. It changes how much of the business the owner still owns, and how much of next year's profit is still theirs, once the money has done its job. If a growth decision is approaching and the funding conversation is moving faster than the sequencing conversation, a fractional CFO earns their place right there, mapping the stack before the first instrument gets chosen. For an independent read on where a business currently sits, booking a discovery call is usually the lowest cost way to find out.

faqs.q: What is the right order to raise capital for a growing Australian SME?
faqs.a: The cheapest capital usually comes first: retained profit, then finance tied to a specific asset or to receivables, then bank term debt sized against serviceability, then mezzanine for any remaining gap. Equity is typically the last option, because it is a permanent share of profit rather than a cost that ends once it is repaid. A capital raise preparation review is a useful way to map the sequence before approaching anyone.

faqs.q: Is equity funding always the most expensive way to fund business growth?
faqs.a: In almost every case, yes. Debt and asset finance carry a cost that ends once the facility is repaid. Equity has no end date. It is a permanent share of every future year of profit, not just the year the capital was needed. That is not a reason to avoid equity altogether, but it is a reason to use it only for the portion of a raise that genuinely cannot be funded any other way.

faqs.q: Why would a bank refuse a loan that a business can clearly afford?
faqs.a: Banks lend against serviceability, a calculation of whether cash flow can comfortably cover repayments, not against how promising the growth opportunity looks. A business can be a strong commercial bet and still fail a serviceability test if the timing of cash inflows does not line up with the loan's repayment schedule. That gap is usually where asset finance or a facility review opens up options a standard term loan would not.

faqs.q: What does a capital raise feasibility assessment actually involve?
faqs.a: It is a structured look at whether the business is ready to raise debt, mezzanine or equity, which instrument genuinely fits the growth plan, and realistically what investors or lenders would pay or lend given the business as it stands today. The Capital Raise Feasibility engagement is built around exactly that question, before any term sheet or lender conversation begins.

faqs.q: Should a business use its own cash or outside finance to fund growth?
faqs.a: Retained profit is the cheapest capital available, so it is usually the first option worth exhausting. The exception is when using it entirely drains the working capital buffer the rest of the business relies on. In that case, financing the growth itself, rather than funding it from the operating account, often protects the business more than it costs.

faqs.q: How does a fractional CFO help a business decide how to fund growth?
faqs.a: A fractional CFO brings the discipline of mapping the full capital stack before any single instrument is chosen, rather than reacting to whichever offer arrives first. That sequence, retained profit, asset finance, bank debt, mezzanine, equity, is often the difference between funding growth well and funding it in a way that costs more than it needed to.

faqs.q: Is mezzanine finance common for Queensland and East Coast SMEs?
faqs.a: It is less common than bank debt, but it fills a real gap for growing businesses that have exhausted senior debt capacity but are not ready, or willing, to give up equity. It costs more than term debt and less than equity, which makes it a useful bridge for the specific portion of a raise that falls between the two.
